How to use this map−
What this shows. This map is a research toolkit for land and environmental defenders — the public databases, records systems and watchdog organisations you can use to investigate the corporations, developers, agencies and money behind the road, mine, pipeline, dam, logging or development threatening a place you’re trying to protect. It groups those tools by what you’re trying to find out: who really owns a company, where the public money goes, a facility’s environmental and legal record, how to pry loose documents, and who owns a parcel of land. It plots them for every jurisdiction where they exist — national, state, county and municipal. To use it, start by clicking your country and then a lit region; open any single entry to read exactly what it can — and can’t — tell you, and lean on the lens pills to the right, or the searchable index below, to narrow the whole map down to the one kind of record a particular fight needs. International bodies — cross-border institutions relevant to land and environmental defence, such as development banks, environmental and human-rights tribunals, and watchdog networks that operate across nations — appear as gold markers; click any to open it, just like a country.

Two ways to filter:
1· Lens pills (right) — each lens is a kind of research: corporate ownership, contracts & money, court records, environmental compliance, FOIA, property, people & networks, monitoring, watchdogs. Selecting one filters the map to that theme so you can see where those resources exist. Below the pills you can narrow further.
2· Index — a directory of the resources on the map. Group & sort it (by country, level, lens…) and search by name.

Navigate. Click a country to zoom in — its regions load and any that hold resources light up. Click a lit region to open its list of research tools, and to drill deeper into its sub-divisions (state → county → municipal), since many records — property, courts, permits — are held locally. Click empty space or zoom out to step back up.

● police, town halls, fire, gov offices, agency HQs — local buildings relevant to different campaigns (records, policing, permits, land use). Facility dots become clickable once you zoom in (about zoom 8) — click one for details (or toggle it off, top-right, to select regions instead). Keep this in mind if a country's highlight won't select at higher zoom levels: a dot is likely intercepting the click, so switch facilities off first. Click a town-hall or government-office dot for its website — that is where municipalities post the planning applications, agendas and permit files for local projects, often earliest of all.

How to read an entry. Every resource spells out what you can and can’t get from it, and ties it to a concrete aim — stopping a development, fighting a polluter, exposing a landlord, following political money. Sources are official government databases or independent watchdogs and newsrooms; every link is live and verified, and gaps are held honestly, never guessed. As of now the index holds roughly 2,780 verified resources across 212 countries and territories, plus cross-border international bodies — there is no honest way to say what fraction of every relevant source on Earth that is (no one has counted them all), so treat it as a large, growing, verified set rather than a finished one; the number climbs with every build.

Note: A resource is placed at the level of the people it can help, not its street address. A law firm based in one town that takes cases anywhere in the state (or an organisation that serves a whole country) is a region-wide source: it appears under “Higher-level / region-wide sources” at every county or region within that reach, even though it is physically local to one place. Its placement reflects who it can serve, not its location. Only genuinely place-bound resources (a county recorder, a single-county firm) sit at the local level.

You don’t have to go it alone
Even with every resource here in hand, you don’t need to be a lone wolf. Local organisations — nonprofits, conservancies, land trusts, community coalitions and the watchdog groups in the lenses above — carry roots and hard-won experience that starting fresh can’t match in time. Reaching out to them for guidance and direction isn’t a detour; it’s often the fastest, wisest first move.

The live projects layer
The dots are real building projects — permits, environmental reviews and licences — harvested automatically from official public records. Many have already been permitted or are under construction, while others are still in review or only proposed — so plenty can still be met before the outcome is decided.

Reading a dot. A solid dot is an exact location from the record; a dashed ring means the source gave no coordinates, so it sits at country, state or town level — open the record to find the exact site. Size and colour both track the project’s rated scale (from its dollar value, area or capacity): bigger dots are larger projects, and the colour shifts with scale too — from cool teal for the smallest, through olive, gold and plum, to warm rust for the largest, landscape-scale projects. Note: a small project in the wrong place can matter more than a large one elsewhere.
▾ A note on how projects are measured
French and Indian permit entries are sized by building floor area, not land footprint — a project crossing a threshold is at least that substantial, whatever acreage it sits on. Some layers carry no numeric size and are shown at map scale by type: Australia (EPBC), Canada (IAAC), Brazil (IBAMA), and U.S. federal reviews (Federal Register, public-land NEPA) — about 12,400 sites, roughly 8% of all mapped.
Global Wire
The modern development machine runs on paper: an environmental review filed, a wetland permit sought, a rezoning buried in a legal ad no one reads. That paperwork is also its weakness — every notice is a comment window, every review a place to intervene, every permit a decision that can be challenged.

Against that machine grew a web of defenders — riverkeepers and land trusts, tribal nations and neighborhood coalitions, wilderness alliances and environmental-law firms that sue for free. They learned that a listed species, a floodplain, a buried document or a company’s own record can stop a project cold.

The fights are everywhere at once — lithium mines and data centers, pipelines and warehouses, LNG terminals and clear-cuts — and they move fast. This land-defense news wire watches for them: the projects entering the pipeline, the companies behind them, and the places worth defending. Find the fight.

▾ Where this data comes from & what's not (yet) in it
Where the live-projects data comes from
Every dot comes from a public, official or established source, harvested automatically and filtered to proposed and under-construction projects only — anything operating, cancelled, shelved or of unknown status is dropped by a fail-safe gate. The feeds:
Who records these. Some layers are built by volunteers and community researchers logging projects they come across — OpenStreetMap’s under-construction sites, the Environmental Justice Atlas, and the Land Matrix land-deal monitor. The rest are official government and research databases the map pulls in automatically. Either way, a project appears only once it has been recorded in one of these public sources — so coverage keeps growing as people and agencies add more.



• Global trackers: Global Energy Monitor (13 trackers — gas, oil & gas extraction, coal terminals, wind, solar, hydro, geothermal, nuclear, iron ore), World Bank projects, IATI development aid, Land Matrix land deals, EJAtlas conflicts.
• At sea: EMODnet Human Activities — the EU’s official marine spatial-data network — feeds planned, approved and under-construction offshore wind farms across European seas (new); GEM’s wind and oil-&-gas trackers already carry offshore projects worldwide, and coastal coal/gas terminals come from GEM’s terminal trackers.
• National registers: US federal EIS notices + BLM/Forest Service NEPA, France Sitadel building permits, UK PlanIt planning applications, Australia EPBC referrals, Canada IAAC assessments, Brazil IBAMA licences, plus PermitStack ($1M+ construction permits, all 50 US states) and city open-data (Chicago, Seattle).
• Portal federations: ~2,200 government open-data portals worldwide speaking seven protocols — CKAN (548), OpenDataSoft (308), GeoNode (274), DKAN (104), uData, generic WFS/GeoServer (987, incl. EU offshore-energy layers), OGC API Features — queried in ~50 languages.
• OpenStreetMap: mapped construction sites worldwide, refreshed on a tile grid.
URLs, API fields and status vocabularies are live-verified before a source ships; gaps are flagged, never papered over.

How to read this as a picture of the world
Live projects blends two kinds of feed. Most markers — led by OpenStreetMap’s under-construction layer, plus the Australia, Canada and World-Bank project registers — show what is being built or assessed right now, whenever it was permitted. The rest are recent permit / notice feeds, each looking back a set window (roughly 45–365 days: US Federal Register 120d · US public-land 180d · UK 180d · France 12 mo). So this is a rolling picture of what is newly permitted plus currently underway — much fuller than a one-month snapshot, but still a sample, not a census: places with no open-data feed, and projects permitted before a feed’s window that aren’t also mapped as under construction, won’t appear. The feeds don’t record completion dates, so the map can’t measure how long a project lasts — but for context, the bigger the project the longer it runs, and almost none finish within the map’s shortest window: US Census figures put a single-family home at ~8 months start-to-completion (the large majority within a year), apartment & commercial buildings at ~17–20 months (mostly over a year), and large infrastructure & extraction (highways, transit, dams, power, mines) at 2–5+ years.

Why a project you know of may be missing. A project appears only if it’s in one of the public feeds above. Small US cities that publish no open permit data often surface only through their state environmental filings: California’s and Washington’s are now pulled in (via their state environmental-review registers — CEQAnet and the SEPA Register), but most other US states and countries have no equivalent feed here yet, so a real local approval elsewhere can stay absent until the site is tagged under construction in OpenStreetMap. The layer also skips small and private work (householder permits, and anything below the OpenStreetMap size floor).

Sources examined but not includable (and why)
Honest accounting of everything evaluated across the build that could not (yet) be added:
• Junar portals (Peru OEFA, Chile Energía Abierta, Costa Rica + 10 more): the API requires per-portal keys that only the operating agency can issue; public keys are referer-locked.
• CoST / OC4IDS infrastructure portals (Honduras SISOCS, Uganda, Ukraine, Malawi, Guatemala): the data standard is real and the portals publish, but no machine-readable endpoint could be live-verified; adding them would mean guessing URLs.
• Western Australia DWER sites: the data license requires written permission.
• HTML-only registers (Germany UVP-Verbund, Netherlands ruimtelijke plannen, England MMO marine licensing, NZ fast-track, Tasmania & NT EPA, Ecuador SUIA, Ontario ERO, Victoria, South Australia SARIG, Mexico SIGEIA, South Africa, Philippines ECC): human-readable registers with no API or export; scraping them would be fragile and against several sites' terms.
• India Parivesh: the clearance API exists but its endpoint has been dormant/unreachable; a fetcher is built and waiting.
• FERC eLibrary: has an API, but it is a docket/document index — filings, orders and comment notices — with no project coordinates. Plotting it would require text-geocoding two million mostly non-geographic documents; the live comment windows are real but do not overcome the no-points gate, so it stays a stub.
• Deep-sea mining geodata held — but fully viewable at the source: no seabed mine is under construction anywhere on Earth yet (the ISA has granted exploration contracts only), and the ISA publishes every exploration-contract area through its DeepData GIS viewer and maps page — view the contract areas, reserved areas and APEIs there directly. They can’t be harvested onto this map because no machine endpoint could be verified and ISA’s terms bar reuse of its shapefiles without written permission. The registry itself is on this map under International bodies (contract list). The live permitting frontier is the U.S. NOAA/DSHMRA route: the first commercial seabed-mining permit fight in history is live right now — TMC’s Clarion-Clipperton application was found in substantial compliance in March 2026 — and it is happening on paper, in public dockets where comments can still be filed: follow it in the Federal Register.
• GEM trackers held (browse them anyway at globalenergymonitor.org): bioenergy (all download branches 404), GIST (no project-status field — the in-process gate can't run), coal-plant retirements & methane sites (operating/emissions data, not a project pipeline), integrated tracker (duplicates the individual ones).
• Other portal protocols (GeoNetwork/CSW, OAI-PMH, PxWeb, NADA, .Stat/SDMX, STAC/THREDDS/ERDDAP, ~1,000 fully-custom sites): these serve metadata, statistics tables or satellite rasters — not project-point data — or have no API at all.
• PermitStack depth & dependency: the binding limit is not the 99 requests/day quota but the free tier's 30-day window — only the last 30 days of permits are available at any request volume, with historical depth starting at a paid tier (every other national feed here runs 45–365 days). And in the spirit of this accounting: the US permit layer leans on a single commercial vendor with a short operating history — a dependency chosen rather than forced, disclosed here alongside the licence and endpoint problems.

So how much am I seeing? There is no honest percentage — no dataset holds the true number of all proposed or under-construction projects on Earth, so any “the map shows X%” figure would be invented. There is, though, one corner where a real, bounded ratio does exist, and the map reports it rather than inventing a global one: US new-residential permits. The US Census Building Permits Survey publishes the national count of housing units authorized each month, so the map's caught US residential permits can be divided by that Census total — a single verifiable coverage ratio. Expect it to be small: the permit layer is deliberately gated to $1M+ projects, so it catches a size-biased sliver of the millions of ordinary units the Census counts. That is the point — one honest, checkable number about a known slice, not a made-up figure about the whole. But an honest picture of the shape of the sample is possible. What the map covers well: large projects (the $1M+ permits, and the $50M / 500-acre / 500-MW tiers), energy and extraction almost everywhere via Global Energy Monitor, and any project that entered a formal environmental or planning review in a covered jurisdiction (US, UK, France, Canada, Australia, Brazil, and the ~2,200 open-data portals). What is thin or missing: small municipal permits below the size floors, the roughly 40 countries with no harvestable register, and anything locked behind a login or published only as un-scrapable HTML (the flagged sources above). So: for a major energy, extraction or reviewed infrastructure project in a covered country, the map is close to comprehensive; for small local developments, or anywhere in an uncovered country, treat it as a partial sample and check the local sources directly. A strong, verifiable sample of the world's project pipeline — not a complete census, which no one has.

Which countries lack a harvestable register? The “roughly 40” is an estimate, not a fixed roll-call — it’s the set of countries where a project or permit register was looked for but none could be machine-harvested. The ones this build actually ran down break into three groups. Behind key-locked Junar portals: Peru, Chile and Costa Rica, plus about ten more agencies on the same platform whose feeds need agency-issued keys (the build logged the count, not a verified country-by-country roster, so they aren’t named individually here). On the CoST / OC4IDS infrastructure standard, with no verifiable endpoint: Honduras, Uganda, Ukraine, Malawi and Guatemala. Published only as un-scrapable HTML, or behind a dormant API: Germany, the Netherlands, England, New Zealand, Ecuador, Canada (Ontario), Mexico, South Africa, the Philippines and India. That is the honestly-documented list; naming a longer roster would mean guessing, so the rest are simply held as “no register found yet.” As each one is found and verified, it moves off this list and onto the map.
